hints: Notice the microphone finds a fixed silent point along its path, which means destructive interference where the path difference is $(n+1/2)\lambda$.
Recall coherence for two-source sound interference needs the same frequency and a constant phase difference, plus similar amplitude for good cancellation.
Ask whether the constant phase difference has to be zero at the loudspeakers, or whether a different fixed starting phase could still be compensated by the path difference to give antiphase arrival.
walkthrough: The no-sound point is a minimum of two-source interference. At the microphone the two sound waves superpose and cancel when they arrive in antiphase.

For the minimum to stay at a fixed position, the interference pattern must be stationary. This requires coherent waves: same frequency $f$ and therefore same wavelength $\lambda$ in the same air, where $v = f\lambda$, and a constant phase difference.
Similar amplitude is also needed in practice, otherwise the resultant cannot be zero when one wave has much larger displacement than the other.

Being emitted exactly in phase is a special case of constant phase difference. If the loudspeakers have a fixed non-zero phase difference, the path difference needed for antiphase arrival simply shifts, but a fixed silent point can still exist.
Therefore in-phase emission is not a necessary condition. This is option A.

options.A: A constant phase difference is enough. The sources do not have to start in phase because a fixed non-zero phase difference still gives a fixed destructive position.
options.B: Similar amplitudes are needed so the two displacements can cancel to near zero at the minimum.
options.C: The same frequency is needed for coherence so the interference minima stay fixed in space.
options.D: The same wavelength is needed so the condition for destructive interference by path difference stays at a fixed point.
